Synthetic data from a profile

Richard Aubrey White

Source: vignettes/synthetic-data.Rmd
synthetic-data.Rmd

csdb makes synthetic data for one table in two steps. A profile summarises the real table with aggregate SQL, under disclosure control. A simulator then draws new rows from the profile. A SyntheticTable holds the contract of the table and a catalogue of fixed datasets, so that a test can name the data it uses.

This vignette works at the level of one table. Two other vignettes build on it:

  • cs9, vignette("synthetic-data", package = "cs9"): synthetic tables, synthetic mode and switchable sources in a surveillance system.
  • norsyss.cs9, vignettes/synthetic-development.Rmd in the private repository niphr/norsyss.cs9: one late task of a real pipeline, run on synthetic inputs alone.

Every chunk here runs on SQLite.

A table to profile

The table holds 600 made-up consultations. Each row is one visit of one person.

library(csdb)
#> csdb 2026.11.7
#> https://niphr.github.io/csdb/
library(data.table)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'data.table'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     %notin%

set.seed(1)
visits <- data.table(
  id = sample(1:150, 600, replace = TRUE),
  date = as.Date("2024-01-01") + sample(0:120, 600, replace = TRUE),
  sex = sample(c("female", "male"), 600, replace = TRUE),
  age = sample(0:95, 600, replace = TRUE),
  consultations = rpois(600, 3),
  municipality = sample(sprintf("m%03d", 1:40), 600, replace = TRUE)
)
visits[1:3, date := as.Date("2024-09-30")]

tab <- DBTable_v9$new(
  dbconfig = list(driver = "SQLite", db = tempfile(fileext = ".sqlite")),
  table_name = "visits",
  field_types = c(
    id = "INTEGER",
    date = "DATE",
    sex = "TEXT",
    age = "INTEGER",
    consultations = "INTEGER",
    municipality = "TEXT"
  ),
  keys = NULL,
  validator_field_types = validator_field_types_blank,
  validator_field_contents = validator_field_contents_blank
)
invisible(tab$create_table())
#> Creating table visits
tab$insert_data(visits)

Three rows move to 2024-09-30, a week with no other visit. Disclosure control has to deal with them below.

Sensitivity levels

Each column gets one of four sensitivity levels. A column that columns does not name is schema_only.

Level What the profile publishes
full the values and their counts; above max_levels, bins for a number and n_distinct for text
coarsen a date by ISO week, a number by bins
schema_only the type and the share of missing values
exclude nothing beyond the field type

profile_table() reads the query, the field types and the keys from the table. profile_query() does the same for any SQL query.

p <- profile_table(
  tab,
  columns = c(
    id = "exclude",
    date = "full",
    sex = "full",
    age = "coarsen",
    consultations = "full"
  ),
  k = 5,
  max_levels = 10,
  group_sizes = list(rows_per_id = "id")
)
p$columns$sex
#> $type
#> [1] "TEXT"
#> 
#> $sensitivity
#> [1] "full"
#> 
#> $missing_share
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $levels
#> [1] "female" "male"  
#> 
#> $n
#> [1] 290 310
p$columns$municipality
#> $type
#> [1] "TEXT"
#> 
#> $sensitivity
#> [1] "schema_only"
#> 
#> $missing_share
#> [1] 0

municipality is schema_only, because columns does not name it. The profile holds no value of it.

Suppression by merge

The profile never writes a count below k. On an ordered dimension, a cell below k merges with its neighbours instead of being removed:

  • Days merge into ISO weeks, then calendar months, then calendar quarters. The column takes the finest resolution at which every cell holds k.
  • Bins of a number merge into runs of adjacent bins. A merged bin keeps the outer breaks of its run.
  • Group sizes merge into ranges of row counts. No exact smallest or largest row count is published.

The three late visits are the only visits in their week, their month and their quarter. Each of those cells holds 3, below k = 5. So date comes out by quarter, and the third quarter joins the second in one run:

names(p$columns$date)
#> [1] "type"          "sensitivity"   "missing_share" "quarters"     
#> [5] "quarters_to"   "n"
data.table(
  from = p$columns$date$quarters,
  to = p$columns$date$quarters_to,
  n = p$columns$date$n
)
#>          from         to     n
#>        <Date>     <Date> <int>
#> 1: 2024-01-01 2024-01-01   456
#> 2: 2024-04-01 2024-07-01   144

consultations has more than max_levels distinct values, so it is published as bins. A number column also records nonnegative, which is TRUE when its minimum is at least 0. The simulator then draws no value below 0.

p$columns$consultations$breaks
#> [1] -0.5  0.5  1.5  2.5  3.5  4.5  5.5  6.5 10.5
p$columns$consultations$nonnegative
#> [1] TRUE
p$group_sizes$rows_per_id
#> $column
#> [1] "id"
#> 
#> $size_from
#> [1] 1 3 4 5 6 7 8
#> 
#> $size_to
#> [1] 2 3 4 5 6 7
#> 
#> $n
#> [1] 33 23 30 27 20  7  6

An unordered cell, such as a level of a TEXT column, cannot merge. A cell below k is removed, and the removed counts are summed into suppressed_n when that sum is at least k.

The profile refuses a torn read

profile_query() reads the data with several aggregate queries, in one read snapshot where the driver gives one. It then checks that the counts of each column, plus its missing values, add up to n_rows. A profile that fails the check is torn, and the function refuses it.

A concurrent write without a snapshot tears a profile. This chunk simulates one. It mocks the internal reader of the missing counts, so that 10 rows are inserted through the same connection just after that read. Every later read then sees 610 rows, and n_rows is 600:

con <- tab$dbconnection$autoconnection
real_read <- csdb:::sql_missing_counts
torn <- testthat::with_mocked_bindings(
  sql_missing_counts = function(con, sql, columns) {
    out <- real_read(con, sql, columns)
    DBI::dbExecute(con, "INSERT INTO visits SELECT * FROM visits LIMIT 10")
    return(out)
  },
  tryCatch(
    profile_query(
      con,
      "SELECT * FROM visits",
      columns = c(sex = "full"),
      field_types = c(sex = "TEXT")
    ),
    error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)
  ),
  .package = "csdb"
)
stopifnot(grepl("Torn profile", torn))
cat(torn, "
")
#> Torn profile: the counts of column sex sum to 610 (610 in cells and 0 missing), but n_rows is 600. The data changed while profile_query() read it.
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM visits")$n
#> [1] 600

The function ends its transaction with a rollback, so the 10 inserted rows are gone again.

Write and read the profile

A profile is a YAML file. read_profile() gives back an identical object.

f <- write_profile(p, tempfile(fileext = ".yaml"))
cat(readLines(f)[1:16], sep = "\n")
#> provenance:
#>   format: 1
#>   source: ~
#>   query: |-
#>     SELECT *
#>     FROM `visits`
#>   driver: SQLiteConnection
#>   profiled_at: '2026-11-07T16:39:33Z'
#>   k: 5
#>   noise: ~
#>   max_levels: 10
#>   csdb_version: 2026.11.7
#> field_types:
#>   id: INTEGER
#>   date: DATE
#>   sex: TEXT
identical(read_profile(f), p)
#> [1] TRUE

The provenance names the query, the driver, k, noise, max_levels and the csdb version. It holds no user name.

What a profile may contain

A profile of real data is a release of aggregates. It MUST have the approval of the data owner before it leaves the restricted environment. That holds for a profile in a package directory, in a test fixture and in a git repository.

Suppression keeps every published count at k or above. It does not decide whether the set of aggregates is safe to publish. That decision is the data owner’s. With noise = list(epsilon = e), the profile adds Laplace noise of scale 1 / e to each count before suppression.

Simulate and compare

simulate_from_profile() draws new rows from the published summaries. It reads the profile only, never the profiled rows.

sim <- simulate_from_profile(p, n = 600, seed = 1)
head(sim)
#>       id       date    sex   age consultations    municipality
#>    <int>     <Date> <char> <int>         <int>          <char>
#> 1:     1 2024-03-20 female    62             3  municipality_3
#> 2:     1 2024-03-02 female    20             4 municipality_10
#> 3:     2 2024-02-17 female    30             6  municipality_3
#> 4:     3 2024-02-20   male    50             5  municipality_7
#> 5:     3 2024-01-23   male    79             1  municipality_9
#> 6:     3 2024-04-02   male    34             4  municipality_9

profile_compare() checks how far the simulation is from the real profile. Profile the simulation with the same columns, k and max_levels first:

s <- profile_data(
  sim,
  field_types = p$field_types,
  columns = c(
    id = "exclude",
    date = "full",
    sex = "full",
    age = "coarsen",
    consultations = "full"
  ),
  k = 5,
  max_levels = 10,
  group_sizes = list(rows_per_id = "id")
)
profile_compare(p, s)
#>            column      property    distance  threshold   pass
#>            <char>        <char>       <num>      <num> <lgcl>
#>  1:          date missing_share 0.000000000 0.05000000   TRUE
#>  2:          date      quarters 0.010000000 0.08666667   TRUE
#>  3:           sex missing_share 0.000000000 0.05000000   TRUE
#>  4:           sex        levels 0.003333333 0.09166667   TRUE
#>  5:           age missing_share 0.000000000 0.05000000   TRUE
#>  6:           age          bins 0.053333333 0.14008333   TRUE
#>  7: consultations missing_share 0.000000000 0.05000000   TRUE
#>  8: consultations          bins 0.063333333 0.10833333   TRUE
#>  9:  municipality missing_share 0.000000000 0.05000000   TRUE
#> 10:            id   group_sizes 0.067543246 0.17045045   TRUE

Each row has its own rule for the threshold:

  • A table of counts, such as levels, quarters, bins or group_sizes: the function draws n_boot multinomial tables of the synthetic size from the real shares. It merges each draw with the k of real. The threshold is the 95th percentile of their distances, plus margin.
  • missing_share: n_boot binomial draws of synth$n_rows rows at the real share. The threshold is the 95th percentile of their distances, plus margin. A share of "suppressed" on either side gives no row.
  • n_distinct: the distance is 0 inside the range that synth$n_rows uniform draws from the real values can reach. The threshold is margin.
  • dependency: the distance is 0 when both profiles agree on holds, otherwise 1. The threshold is 0.
  • A summary of real that synth lacks, or holds in a form that does not align: distance 1, threshold margin.

For a table of counts, a smaller simulation gets a wider threshold. No draw models the noise that noise adds to a profile.

A SyntheticTable

A SyntheticTable holds the contract of one table: its field types, its keys, validator_field_contents and named invariants. Every data.table that it returns passed $validate().

An invariant is a function(d) or a function(d, world). It returns TRUE, or a message that says why d fails.

dir <- tempfile("visits-")
dir.create(dir)
write_profile(p, file.path(dir, "profile.yaml"))

ft <- p$field_types
invariants <- list(
  age_nonnegative = function(d) {
    if (all(d$age >= 0, na.rm = TRUE)) TRUE else "age is negative."
  }
)
st <- synthetic_table_from_dir(
  dir,
  name = "visits",
  field_types = ft,
  invariants = invariants
)
print(st$random(n = 5, seed = 3))
#>       id       date    sex   age consultations    municipality
#>    <int>     <Date> <char> <int>         <int>          <char>
#> 1:     1 2024-02-15   male    77             2 municipality_10
#> 2:     1 2024-02-18 female    89             3  municipality_7
#> 3:     1 2024-02-20 female    87             4  municipality_3
#> 4:     1 2024-03-19   male    33             2  municipality_5
#> 5:     2 2024-03-16   male    56             2  municipality_7

$random() with seed = NULL draws a seed and reports it in a message, so a failure can be replayed.

Named datasets

A test SHOULD name the dataset it uses. $add_dataset() stores a recipe in datasets.yaml. A recipe holds n, seed, overrides, the md5 of the world as world_md5, the row count as rows, and the md5 of the data. The name default is the generator output at seed = 1 and n = 1000. A generator that chooses its own size uses n = NULL there.

world <- list(sex = c("female", "male"))
st$add_dataset(
  "default",
  n = 1000,
  seed = 1,
  description = "The generator output at seed 1.",
  world = world
)
st$add_dataset(
  "all_female",
  n = 200,
  seed = 2,
  description = "Every row is female.",
  overrides = list(sex = "female"),
  world = world
)
cat(readLines(file.path(dir, "datasets.yaml")), sep = "\n")
#> - name: default
#>   kind: recipe
#>   'n': 1000
#>   seed: 1
#>   description: The generator output at seed 1.
#>   overrides: []
#>   world_md5: 33e42b7138d2f5c7ae76e6e5ff72ff42
#>   rows: 1000
#>   md5: 9fd7b6d59c58c5bbe02b75bb22dc347b
#> - name: all_female
#>   kind: recipe
#>   'n': 200
#>   seed: 2
#>   description: Every row is female.
#>   overrides:
#>     sex: female
#>   world_md5: 33e42b7138d2f5c7ae76e6e5ff72ff42
#>   rows: 200
#>   md5: 03a2fe75d8d608e93a7abeaa73426476

A handmade dataset is a CSV file in handmade/. Each column is read as text and converted to its field type. An empty cell is NA.

dir.create(file.path(dir, "handmade"))
writeLines(
  c(
    "id,date,sex,age,consultations,municipality",
    "1,2024-01-01,female,40,2,m001",
    "2,2024-01-02,male,,1,m002"
  ),
  file.path(dir, "handmade", "two_visits.csv")
)
st$list_datasets()
#>          name     kind     n  seed                     description
#>        <char>   <char> <int> <int>                          <char>
#> 1:    default   recipe  1000     1 The generator output at seed 1.
#> 2: all_female   recipe   200     2            Every row is female.
#> 3: two_visits handmade    NA    NA                            <NA>
print(st$dataset("two_visits"))
#>       id       date    sex   age consultations municipality
#>    <int>     <Date> <char> <int>         <int>       <char>
#> 1:     1 2024-01-01 female    40             2         m001
#> 2:     2 2024-01-02   male    NA             1         m002

$dataset() regenerates a recipe. When the md5 of the world equals world_md5, it checks the row count against rows and the md5 against md5:

nrow(st$dataset("all_female", world = world))
#> [1] 200
st$check_hashes(world = world)
#>          name   pass
#>        <char> <lgcl>
#> 1:    default   TRUE
#> 2: all_female   TRUE

The hash check after a generator change

A change of the generator changes the data of every recipe. The hash check then stops, and the error names the table and the dataset. Here a new generator draws 1 to 10 consultations in place of the profile:

changed <- function(profile, n, seed, world) {
  d <- simulate_from_profile(profile, n = n, seed = seed, world = world)
  d[, consultations := sample(1:10, .N, replace = TRUE)]
  return(d)
}
st2 <- synthetic_table_from_dir(
  dir,
  name = "visits",
  field_types = ft,
  invariants = invariants,
  generator = changed
)
st2$dataset("all_female", world = world)
#> Error:
#> ! SyntheticTable visits, dataset 'all_female': the regenerated data does not match the md5 in datasets.yaml. The generator, the profile or the overrides changed.

After a deliberate change, delete the recipe from datasets.yaml and add it again with $add_dataset(). A test that reads the dataset then sees the new data.

For a world other than the recipe’s, $dataset() validates the data, does not check the md5, and says so in a message.
